newsitem.title: USA: Digital TV talks continue, accord could come soon.
newsitem.headline: Digital TV talks continue, accord could come soon.

text.p: Representatives from the television broadcasters and computer industries remained in negotiations late Monday over a broadcast standard for a new generation of high-definition digital TV, sources said.
But an official familar with the talks expressed optimism, saying he expected an agreement shortly.
"We expect something imminently," said Paul Misener, an Intel Corp manager. He added, however: "It ain't over 'til it's over."
The current talks are being held in Washington.

Officials from the two sides have held talks over the past month to iron out differences that would pave the way for the roll out of advanced digital TV broadcasts. The system offers cinema-quality pictures and CD-quality sound.

The Federal Communications Commission proposed to mandate an industry standard in May that was developed by an advisory panel that included representatives from the entertainment, broadcaster, electronic and computer industries. The proposed standard took more than eight years to develop.
But computer companies, led by Microsoft Corp., complained afterward that the proposed technology works poorly with computers and would stifle the convergence of TV and computer technologies.
The long-promised convergence would let consumers watch TV and surf the Internet via the same "smart box."
Hollywood directors, actors and cinematographers also were unhappy. They argued that the new screen's shape would mutilate the images in wide-screen films.
The parties involved in the ongoing talks have imposed a gag order over the discussions, so it is not clear what type of accord, if any, might be shaping up.

The negotiations were initiated after a request last month from FCC Commissioner Susan Ness, who is seeking a resolution to the dispute. She set a Nov. 25 deadline for the negotiators to reach agreement, although that date is not legally binding.

The proposed standard has faced rough sledding at the FCC, where chairman Reed Hundt has voiced reservations over mandating an industry standard that eventually could become obsolete and stifle innovation.
